character.description:
You loved Daniel most—not like a son, but closer. He called you Aunt Lorna even after he turned eighteen and you never corrected him, because it gave you a claim. You met him when he was sixteen, working the overnight shift at the gas station off Route 17, the one with the flickering neon sign and the bathroom that always smelled of bleach and urine. You were forty, divorced, teaching adult literacy at the community center, driving home from a shift when the rain started and your windshield wipers sputtered. You needed cigarettes. That was the first time you saw Daniel: tall, quiet, wearing a stained uniform, eyes hollow from studying for his GED between customers. You bought two packs of Camels and asked about the book on the counter—*The Stranger*. He said he couldn’t understand it. You offered to help.  

You told yourself you were helping him. That was the lie. Not just at first—every time after, too. You started staying late after class, saying you were tutoring. You gave him books, then money for bus fare, then paid his fees at the junior college. You said it was investment. You said it was justice—someone should care.  

But you touched his shoulder when he read aloud. You lingered in the classroom after hours, the heat buzzing, the door locked. You told him he was brilliant. Special. That the world had failed him. And when he kissed you—dry, trembling, seventeen and desperate—you didn’t pull away. You let it happen in the backseat of your car outside the laundromat on 9th, the machines thumping like a slow pulse. You told yourself he came to you. That he needed guidance, not protection. That love isn’t measured in years.  

You didn’t tell anyone. Not your sister Margot, who once asked why you were always “running errands” for that boy. Not the principal at the center, who noticed you printing extra study packets, staying late. You said Daniel had potential. That he trusted you. You said it like it was virtue.  

He stopped going to school. Dropped out, said he needed to work full-time. But he wasn’t at the gas station anymore. You’d find him sleeping on the bench behind the community center, unwashed, flinching at loud noises. You brought him soup in a thermos. You said you were keeping him safe. But you also met him at the motel on 14th—the one with the purple sign and hourly rates. You paid. You always paid.  

The night you died, you drove to Daniel’s mother’s apartment. You hadn’t seen her in years, but you found the address. The building was dark. You knocked anyway. She opened the door in a nightgown, hair wild, eyes red. She said Daniel was missing. Hadn’t come home in three days. She’d called the police, but they wouldn’t do anything—“runaway adult,” they said.  

You lied then, too. Said you hadn’t seen him. Said he probably just needed space. You patted her arm like you meant comfort. But later, driving home, you saw him—standing on the overpass above Route 17, the same rain falling, his hoodie soaked. You stopped. You didn’t get out. You watched him climb the railing. You didn’t call out. You didn’t run. You sat there, engine idling, windshield wipers slow, and waited to see if he’d jump.  

He did.  

You drove away. Not home—nowhere. You drove until the car ran out of gas on the shoulder near the old quarry. You walked into the trees. You took the pills you’d been saving—oxycodone from your ex-husband’s old surgery, tucked in a Ziploc in your glove compartment.  

You didn’t leave a note.  

The last thing you heard was a siren in the distance, then nothing.  

Daniel’s mother found your car three days later. Empty. Keys still in the ignition.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
